correctness.rationale: Positive diagonal similarity of a detailed-balance migration matrix gives a symmetric operator; transpose and cyclic determinant invariance prove entire-period cospectrality for every number of positive diagonal seasons. Conversely, positive diagonal profiles concentrating to rank-one habitat projectors isolate any simple directed cycle product as the limiting Perron root. Equality for all lengths 3 through n forces cycle balance, symmetric support and a detailed-balance measure by path ratios. This handles zeros, singular migration and period boundaries. In a positive three-habitat example, exact fractions yield min(R^2 1)-max(F^2 1)=10651/10000>0; nonnegative matrix row-sum bounds certify strict growth separation. The package verifier reconstructs the matrices, full characteristic polynomials and bounds; computation does not substitute for the general proof. A common scaling c=17/27 of each season gives an exact upper bound below 1 on the squared forward multiplier and an exact lower bound above 1 on the squared reverse multiplier, certifying opposite deterministic persistence outcomes.

originality.rationale: Accessible full primary sources provide cyclic-permutation invariance, temporal fitness–dispersal frameworks, and diagonal symmetrizability in period-two evolutionary dispersal, but the compared published claims do not imply the present iff criterion for arbitrary positive seasonal calendars, its at-most-n converse test or its minimal positive three-habitat reversal witness. The known Kolmogorov cycle criterion is expressly credited and not counted as novel. An older equivalent spectral statement remains an acknowledged priority risk.
residual_risks: Historical priority remains provisional: other matrix-product or dynamical-population literature might encode the same iff under different vocabulary.
Nonreversible networks may still have special calendars with equal roots; the theorem concerns equality for all positive profiles, not generic profiles.
The empirical suitability of diagonal local growth and fixed migration is outside the theorem.

value.rationale: In periodically changing spatial populations, dependence of long-run growth on reversing the direction of environmental cycling is a natural and operationally meaningful question, not a decorative invariant. The theorem gives an exact structural answer, distinguishes directional migration circulation from arbitrary habitat growth variation, bounds the length needed for a diagnostic calendar by the habitat count, and proves that three habitats and three seasons are the minimal setting for a strict observable difference. These are motivated all-dimensional facts with a sharp finite physical-model benchmark, not a recomputation of a known numerical table. Indeed a common rational scaling of all three seasonal habitat profiles places the forward and reversed period multipliers on opposite sides of one, so calendar direction changes the population extinction-versus-growth verdict in the specified linear model.
